subject: medicine
title: Cholestatic liver enzymes, hepatic synthetic function, and obstructive jaundice

steps.tx: Synthesis and shedding of canalicular ecto-enzymes accelerate rapidly in response to mechanical bile duct obstruction or canalicular stasis. Elevation of serum **alkaline phosphatase** represents de novo enzyme synthesis triggered by detergent bile acids acting on the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes and cholangiocytes. Because isoenzymes also originate from osteoblasts during active bone remodeling, intestinal enterocytes, and the placenta during pregnancy, isolated elevations mandate confirmation of hepatobiliary origin through complementary biochemical testing.
steps.say: Synthesis of canalicular membrane enzymes accelerates in response to biliary duct obstruction. Elevation of alkaline phosphatase reflects de novo enzyme production induced by bile acid retention. Because circulating isoenzymes also originate from bone remodeling, the intestines, and the placenta, isolated elevations require confirmation of biliary origin before initiating invasive investigations.

steps.tx: Enzymatic confirmation of hepatobiliary origin for elevated alkaline phosphatase relies on measuring microsomally localized transferases. Circulating **GGT** (gamma-glutamyl transferase) is located in the endoplasmic reticulum of biliary epithelial cells and hepatocytes, elevating alongside alkaline phosphatase in cholestatic disorders. Because GGT remains completely normal in primary bone pathologies, finding an elevated level definitively confirms a hepatobiliary source. Furthermore, hepatic microsomal induction by heavy alcohol consumption, phenytoin, or barbiturates elevates GGT in the absence of cholestasis.
steps.say: Confirming a hepatobiliary origin for elevated alkaline phosphatase relies on measuring biliary transferases. Gamma-glutamyl transferase, or GGT, is localized within biliary epithelial cells and hepatocytes. Because GGT remains entirely normal in bone disease, an elevated level confirms a hepatobiliary source. Alcohol consumption and enzyme-inducing medications also stimulate GGT synthesis independently of cholestasis.

steps.tx: Monitoring hepatic production of short-lived coagulation factors provides the most sensitive, rapid assessment of evolving acute hepatocellular synthetic failure. Prolongation of **prothrombin time** (or elevated INR) directly mirrors diminished hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Because factor VII exhibits an exceptionally short circulating half-life of only four to six hours, prothrombin time elongates within hours of acute parenchymal necrosis, serving as a cardinal prognostic marker in King's College criteria for acute liver failure.
steps.say: Monitoring short-lived coagulation factor synthesis provides the fastest measure of acute liver failure. Prolongation of prothrombin time reflects reduced production of vitamin K-dependent factors. Because factor VII has a circulating half-life of only five hours, prothrombin time lengthens within hours of acute hepatic injury, serving as a critical prognostic indicator.

rows: Earliest factor to deplete; rapid INR rise

steps.tx: Quantification of circulating plasma proteins synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes reflects long-term functional reserve in chronic parenchymal disorders. Circulating **serum albumin** possesses an extended half-life of approximately twenty days, meaning that levels remain entirely preserved in acute fulminant hepatic necrosis. In contrast, gradual decline below three point five grams per decilitre indicates sustained synthetic exhaustion characteristic of chronic cirrhosis. Concurrently, declining oncotic pressure contributes directly to the formation of peripheral pedal oedema and ascites.
steps.say: Measuring circulating plasma proteins reflects long-term functional reserve in chronic liver disease. Serum albumin has a long half-life of three weeks, remaining normal during acute hepatic injury. In contrast, progressive decline below three point five grams per decilitre reflects chronic synthetic failure in cirrhosis, lowering oncotic pressure and causing ascites.

steps.tx: Impairment of bile formation or canalicular flow leads to systemic retention of bilirubin, bile salts, and cholesterol. Presentation of **cholestatic jaundice** produces the classic clinical triad of dark amber urine containing conjugated bilirubin, pale clay-coloured stools lacking stercobilin, and intractable pruritus caused by dermal bile salt and pruritogen deposition. Etiologies divide into intrahepatic causes (primary biliary cholangitis, drug-induced cholestasis, viral hepatitis) and extrahepatic mechanical ductal obstruction.
steps.say: Impairment of bile excretion causes systemic accumulation of bilirubin, bile salts, and cholesterol. Manifesting as cholestatic jaundice, patients present with dark urine containing direct bilirubin, pale clay-coloured stools lacking stercobilin, and severe pruritus. Causes divide into intrahepatic medical cholestasis and extrahepatic mechanical ductal obstruction.

steps.tx: Physical impedance to bile flow within the extrahepatic biliary tree generates upstream ductal dilatation and retrograde reflux of conjugated pigment. Clinical presentation of **obstructive jaundice** stems primarily from choledocholithiasis, cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic head carcinoma, or benign biliary strictures. Painful jaundice with fever and rigors defines acute cholangitis (Charcot triad), whereas painless, progressively deepening jaundice accompanied by a palpable, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) strongly indicates malignant periampullary or pancreatic head neoplasia.
steps.say: Physical obstruction of extrahepatic bile ducts produces ductal dilatation and retrograde pigment reflux. Developing obstructive jaundice arises from gallstones, bile duct tumours, or pancreatic head cancer. Painful jaundice with rigors indicates acute cholangitis. Conversely, painless progressive jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder points toward malignant periampullary obstruction.

steps.tx: Comprehensive clinical evaluation distinguishes isolated biochemical derangements from true deterioration of vital functional reserves. Assessing **hepatic synthetic function** requires monitoring prothrombin time, serum albumin, and neurological status (evaluating hepatic encephalopathy), which constitute the foundational components of the Child-Pugh and MELD scoring systems. Unlike transaminase levels, which merely reflect acute cytolysis, synthetic indices directly predict surgical risk, perioperative mortality, and urgent indications for liver transplantation.
steps.say: Comprehensive clinical assessment distinguishes simple enzyme elevation from loss of vital metabolic capacity. Evaluating hepatic synthetic function focuses on prothrombin time, serum albumin, and neurological status, forming the core of Child-Pugh and MELD scores. Unlike aminotransferases that track cell membrane injury, synthetic markers directly predict survival and transplant urgency.

steps.tx: Immediate non-invasive anatomical imaging serves as the essential first triage step to distinguish surgical from medical jaundice. Performing emergency **abdominal ultrasonography** achieves over ninety percent sensitivity for demonstrating dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary ducts (common bile duct calibre exceeding six millimetres). Demonstrating ductal dilatation confirms extrahepatic mechanical obstruction, mandating subsequent cross-sectional magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or therapeutic ERCP. Conversely, normal non-dilated ducts indicate intrahepatic medical cholestasis or hepatocellular jaundice.
steps.say: Non-invasive imaging serves as the vital initial triage step separating surgical from medical jaundice. Performing abdominal ultrasonography demonstrates dilated biliary ducts when common bile duct diameter exceeds six millimetres. Identifying dilated ducts confirms mechanical obstruction requiring magnetic resonance imaging or ERCP. Non-dilated ducts point toward intrahepatic cholestasis or parenchymal liver injury.

nodes.label: Dilated ducts: Extrahepatic obstruction -> MRCP / ERCP
Non-dilated ducts: Intrahepatic cholestasis -> Serology / Biopsy
